sections.content: The course covers the core of investment management: the risk and return tradeoff, margin trading and short selling, capital allocation, diversification and optimal risky portfolios, CAPM, factor models, performance evaluation, efficient markets and behavioral finance. Towards the end it also looks at newer data and technique-based trading strategies. The course is quite tough and quantitative, but it is very relevant because it teaches you how to allocate money across assets, how to price securities and how to judge whether a portfolio manager is doing a good job. There is a practical side as well: we build portfolios in Excel and do a case study during class, which helps a lot to make the theory concrete. The slides are the main material and the textbook is optional.

The PowerPoint slides are often overcrowded with text and formulas, making them difficult to follow as key points are not clearly highlighted. Additionally, the instructor prefers explaining calculations by handwriting them on paper and projecting them on the screen. However, the handwriting is sometimes unclear, and the alignment of the paper on the projector is often not adjusted properly, which makes it hard to read.

The course includes four group assignments, with one due every two weeks. This becomes especially challenging when dealing with uncooperative group members, as the workload unfairly increases for responsible students.

The midterm exam consists of 50 MCQ, which are calculation-based but not overly difficult. However, the final exam is much more demanding, with 20 LQ  , many of which include multiple sub-questions (a, b, c, d).

sections.teaching:

As a vested interest, I personally definitely think it's a good grade class, but objectively speaking, Mukherjee said in the first class that an OVERALL of 90% or above is required to get an A; at the same time there are a lot of QFINs/RMBIs/GBUSs in the class together, and the competition is stiff.
But! If you have a good foundation in FINA 2303, are interested in the subject, and are motivated to understand the course content carefully, I would basically say that Mukerjee's 3103 is a good grade class.
But the grading is 100% fair.

作为既得利益者，我个人肯定是觉得非常好龟，但是客观来讲，mukherjee在第一节课上说，overall在90%以上才能拿到A；与此同时一起上课的人也有很多的QFIN/RMBI/GBUS，竞争是比较激烈的。

Prof. AOYAGI focuses more on math, so he spent an amount of time deriving formulaes like CAPM, Port. frontier, Bond durations, so on so forth, helping us to understand the essence behind these theories deeper.
His teaching is actually clear and logical, but inadequately paced. He didn't arrange any makeup classes for the first two Fridays, and he kept teaching too many details at the first few slides where we are supposed to be quite familiar (ISOM 2500 and FINA 2303 related stuff) or self-learnt by our own (basically intro. to the markets, involving very little calculations). The 4 group assignments may take a little time if you aren't familiar with Excel. They are more practical and related to real-world problems, e.g. running regressions to confirm whether the results are in line with the model prediction. Interestingly, most of the time the answer is a big "no", so it shows the limitations of the models we've learned in class. Anyway, the skill-set to identify which model to use, which evaluation metric to stick onto, and to back-check the model validity is more important than learning the models themselves. Know how to do is a computer thing, but know what to do needs human brain power.

Strictly speaking though, we aren't really there yet as in the real world it involves grabbing information and identifying problems by ourselves. In the assignments all these are already done by the TA before they are released to us.

Overall workload manageable even if you do the assignments alone - each assignment only takes around 1 or 2 hours. That's why our group ended up just doing them individually and cross-checking our answers at the end. And I believe most of the groups can get perfect score for all 4 assignments except for a few outlier groups.

BTW try to familiarize yourself with Excel when you have the chance (esp if you find yourself using a hell lot of time in the assignments). If you don't know how to use basic functions such as Goal Seek, Excel Solver, etc, spend some time understanding them. In the workplace you can't say, "I'm not gonna spend time analyzing thousands of stocks using Excel". You just HAVE to, not to mention our TA has already done some preparatory work in the Excel file and we aren't even starting from the raw data.

Preparation for the exams should be manageable. Utpal provides a number of key questions from the textbooks in the revision session and I find going though them good enough for the exams. But again make sure that you budget your time carefully and don't get stuck at 1 particular question.
